source_title: Provenance update
authors: Gilles de Corbeil 1140?-1224 (Gilles de Corbeil [Aegidius Corboliensis])
other_info: The final two works, De judicio pulsuum and De urinis, are the work of Gilles de Corbeil [Aegidius Corboliensis], not Giles of Rome. Fol. 1-43v were the product of a copist who must have studied in Paris between 1286 and 1300, according to Laurence Moulinier-Brogi, “La Practica fratris du ms. Munich, Clm 267 : une lecture d’Avicenne par un religieux au xiiie siècle?” Archives d'histoire doctrinale et littéraire du Moyen Âge 84(2017) 157-312, at 177 : “...un petit codex de 53 folios daté d’entre 1286 et 1300 et mutilé en son début, qui doit sa relative notoriété au fait qu’il transmet une version du Thesaurus Pauperum de Petrus Hispanus. Outre ce célèbre texte, il renferme des textes anonymes : De virtute herbarum, De judicio pulsarum, De urinis, et la Concordantia Auctorum aux f. 25-42.” Moulinier-Brogi says (n. 94): “M. H. Rocha da Pereira a souligné que le copiste doit avoir au minimum étudié à Paris, puisqu’il complète la recette ‘De gutta rosacea’ par l’information suivante : ‘Hoc unguento usus fuit Magister Matheus et habuit ab Abbate qui dicebatur Potriaus, qui legit Cirurgiam super Pontem Parvum, Parisius’ (Obras de Maria Helena Rocha da Pereira, VI : Latin medieval, Fundaçao Calouste Gulbenkian, Imprensa da Universidade de oimbra 2014, p. 45, n. 1).” On fol. 54r, a (14th-century?) price, ‘xij s[solidi] par[isiensis]’.

source_title: "Préparations pharmaceutiques commandées par Louis XI", Bibliothèque de l'école des chartes, 55 (1894), pp. 721-722
titles: Incipiunt experimenta Bubikir Eirasis filii Zaccarie in doloribus juncturarum.; Practica puerorum (); Tractatus Bubukir Eirasis filii Zaccarie in enarracione diversarum medicinarum expertarum a diversis actoribus medicine inventarum, qui intitulatur Experimentatio medicinalis.; Tractatus Bubukir Eirasis filii Zaccarie de preparatione medicinarum, ut sine horribilitate saporis et odoris sumantur; Tractatus ejusdem qui nuncupatur liber presciencie Ypocratis, continens xxiii propositiones
authors: Rāzī, Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Zakarīyā, 865?-925? (Razi)
other_info:
M. Claudin, libraire, nous a communiqué une copie de plusieurs traités du médecin Razi, faite à Paris en 1471, qui avait appartenu au xviiie siècle à Claude-Bernard Rousseau, auditeur des comptes, et plus
anciennement à « Monsieur de Massac, médecin à Orléans. » Le livre se termine par cette souscription :
« Explicit tractatus qui dicitur liber presciencie Ypocratis. Et in hoc
completur liber experimentorum Bubukir Eirasis filii Zaccarie, qui
completus fuit Parisius anno Domini millésimo quadringentesimo
septuagesimo primo, die vicesima mensis decembris. » Une assez curieuse particularité remarquée dans ce volume par M. Claudin, c'est la mention de la préparation de deux recettes qui fut
ordonnée par le roi Louis XI.
En marge de la page 108, en regard de ce passage : « Aliud mirabile
contra ventositatem fořtem, R/ : anisi cimini satureie..., » on lit ces mots : « 13a septembris, Rex precepit facere hic notatum. »
Un peu plus loin, sur la marge de la page 124, à côté du : « Capitulum secundum de medicinis ad ornatum faciei. Medicamen ad maculas magnas removendas et ad cutem subtiliendam et albificandam.
R/ : farine lupinorum partes quatuor..., » une main contemporaine de
la copie a tracé ces mots : « 13 septembris 1478, Rex precepit facere hic notatum. »
Ces deux notes peuvent être attribuées au médecin ou à l'apothicaire du roi Louis XI.
provenance: Massac, Raymond de (Monsieur de Massac, médecin à Orléans); Rousseau, Claude-Bernard (1648-1720)  (Claude-Bernard Rousseau); Claudin, A. (Anatole), 1833-1906 [ 1894	]

Ina a long essay devoted to the manuscript, Leopold Delisle identified the owner, named as 'Blanche' several times in the text, as Blanche de France, Duchess of Orleans (1328-70).  It was Kathleen Mornad who first suggested in 1961 that Delisle's conclusion should be reconsidered because the style of the illustration of the Spencer volume parallelized that of such earlier Parisian manuscripts as the Life of St. Denis, presented to King Philip V (older brother of Charles IV) in 1317.  Virginia Wylie Egbert subsequently identified 'Blanche' as Blanche of Burgundy, in this way bringing into harmony the style of the illustration and the etxtual contents of the manuscript.

manuscript_binding: "Eighteenth-century brown calf with blind tooling and gilded spine decorations; green endpapers with arabesques stenciled in gold"
other_info: "This Book of Hours was produced in France, likely in Paris, around 1420. It contains a calendar, in French, with Parisian saints (fols. 1r-12v), followed by the Gospel Lessons (fols. 13r-16v), and the Obsecro te and O intemerata (fols. 17r-23r). The core of the book is composed of the Hours of the Virgin of the Use of Rome (fols. 25r-77v); the Penitential Psalms, Litany and Prayers (fols. 79r-94r); the Hours of the Cross (fols. 94v-97r); the Hours of the Holy Spirit (fols. 97v-100r); and the Office of the Dead (fols. 100v-129v). Each of these five major sections is introduced by a large miniature representing, respectively, the Annunciation (fol. 25r), Kind David in Prayer (fol. 79r), the Crucifixion (fol. 94v), Pentecost (fol. 97v), and a Burial Scene (fol. 100v). The first four of these miniatures have diapered backgrounds. The style of the miniatures is typical of Parisian illumination of the second and third decades of the fifteenth century. The style of the miniatures is reminiscent of the so-called Luçon Master."

[...] Le volume a été recouvert au XVIIe siècle d'une riche reliure et on a, à cette époque, ajouté en tête un feuillet de vélin sur lequel sont peintes les armoiries de Pierre de Guerchois, procureur général au Parlement de Rouen, mort en 1692.
other_info: Le volume débute par un calendrier en 12 feuillets; les noms des saints et des fêtes sont écrites en lettres d'or, en lettres rouges et en lettres bleues; ces noms sont écrits en français. Les diverses prières à la Vierge, les offices, les psaumes, etc., sont précédés de 6 ff. contenant le début des quatre Évangiles. Cette première partie du manuscrit se termine par diverses prières en français. Les 16 derniers feuillets contiennent diverses prières en l'honneur des saints. Ce manuscrit est richement décoré et enluminé. Toutes les pages du volume sont entourées de larges bordures avec arabesques formées de traits à la plume avec feuilles et fleurs en or, en rouge et en bleu. Ces bordures sont séparées de la marge latérale par un double filet, l'un d'or, l'autre blanc, bleu et rouge. Les bordures du calendrier sont ornées en outre de 24 petites miniatures de forme ronde représentant les signes du Zodiaque et les diverses occupations de chaque mois. Les miniatures sont au nombre de 43, dont 16 grandes et 27 de plus petite dimension. Les grandes miniatures représentent : Saint Jean dans l'île de Pathmos; la Salutation angélique; la Visitation; la Nativité; l'Annonciation aux bergers; l'Adoration des rois mages; la Circoncision; la Fuite en Égypte; le Couronnement de la Vierge; David en prières; la Crucifixion; la Pentecôte; l'Office des Morts; l'Enterrement; la Vierge et l'enfant Jésus; le Jugement dernier.  Les bordures de ces miniatures sont très riches et comprennent chacune 2 petites miniatures carrées dont le sujet se rapporte à celui de la grande miniature; c'est ainsi que dans la miniature représentant l'Adoration des rois mages on remarque les caxaliers et les chameliers apportant les présents; dans la bordure de la Fuite en Égypte figurent Hérode et le Massacre des Innocents, etc.    Attirons l'attention sur la peinture qui représente David et Bethsabée; contrairement à l'histoire biblique, la scène se passe dans une salle. Nous donnons la reproduction de cette page du manuscrit.   Les miniatures en tête de l'Office des Morts sont particulièrement intéressantes. Elles représentent, la première la Messe funèbre dans une église tendue de noir; le dais et l'autel sont recouverts de draperies d'azur semées de fleurs de lis d'or; les chapes des moines, les cierges, sont également garnis d'écus aux armes de France. La seconde nous montre l'enterrement dans une cimetière; au fond on aperçoit l'âme du défunt emportée au ciel par un ange qui éloigne le démon. Les miniatures de plus petite dimension représentent les Évangélistes, différents saints et saintes et plusieurs scènes de la vie du Christ. Toutes ces peintures sont l'œuvre d'artistes français et sont empreintes de la distinction qui caractérise les miniatures exécutées par les enlumineurs parisiens.

places: Rouen, Normandy, France, Europe; Paris, France, Europe
manuscript_binding: Sewn on three bands and bound in 17th-century plain red-brown leather, incorporating a fragment of a 15th century manuscript [no further information].
other_info: Written in black ink in a formal gothic bookhand, "below top line"; rubrics in red, psalm titles usually in gold, canticle titles usually in red, the calendar in black, red, and blue. the text frequently strengthened, with some passages erased and re-written in the Middle Ages [sic].  Ten large historiated initials, six- to eleven lines high, each accompanied by a partial or full border of foliage and animals.  Probably illuminated in Paris, presumably for the woman depicted in the initial on fol. 188r, who doubtless lived in Rouen given the references to events there in the calendar.  The writing of the calendar must post-date 1247, when the feast of St. Eligius (1 December) was raised to a "triplex", and it must presumably also pre-date 1280, when the feast of St Ansbert (9 February) was similarly raised.  Stylistically the illumination can be dated to the 1260s.  14th-15th century additions suggest the manuscript was owned in the Bouches-du-Rhône region of southern France.

other_info: Superbe livre d'heures [...] dont la très belle ornementation est due à un des meilleurs artistes miniaturistes parisiens de cette époque. [...] d'une belle écriture gothique, et réglés avec soin, il a toutes ses pages, sans exception, illustrées par de gracieuses bordures où les rinceaux de feuillages, les animaux, les grotesques, les fleurs et les fruits, se combinent avec un goût parfait aux compartiments à fonds d'or, à fonds de couleur, de toutes nuances et de toutes formes. Soixante-treize miniatures traitées avec une grande délicatesse décorent ses principaux feuillets. Les vingt-quatre premières sont particulières au calendrier et représentent les douze signes du Zodiaque et les diverses occupations de chacun des mois de l'année. Parmi les quarante-neuf suivantes, quinze d'entre elles occupent la presque totalité d'u  feuillet, sont entièrement entourées par un encadrement à rinceaux et ont pour sujets les principales scènes du Nouveau Testament. Citons: S. Jean l'Évangéliste; la Visitation; le Baiser de Judo, l'Annonciation aux bergers, la Circoncision, le Couronnement de la Vierge, le roi David, Job sur son fumier et un charmant portrait de la Sainte Vierge. Le volume se termine par le propre de saints. Remarquons: S. Michel, S. Germain, S. Jean-Baptiste, S. Jacques, S. Christophe, S. Nicolas, Ste Geneviève, Ste Appoline, S. Eustache, Ste Agnès, etc., tous ces petits portraits sont très soignés dans leur composition. L'analyse du calendrier nous permet de penser que ce beau manuscrit a dû être exécuté à Paris; on y remarque en effet les principaux saints du diocèse: S. Marcel, S. Germain, Ste Geneviève cités trois fois, S. Eleuthère, S. Denis, S. Victor, S. Christophe, Ste Magdelaine, S. Landry, S. Étienne, etc. etc., -- Le 239e feuillet a été légèrement maculé. [PLATE]

other_info: Manuscripts of Aristotle are extremely rare on the market, especially ones with such impressive institutional provenance as the present copy. The Nicomachean Ethics is widely considered to be one of the most important of philosophical works: in it Aristotle outlines the theory of virtuous character based on the idea of finding a golden mean, along with valuable insights about friendship, courage, generosity and justice. Its influence in the European Middle Ages cannot be overstated, and one of the primary translations of the text was carried out - apparently at the request of Thomas Aquinas - by the Flemish Dominican William of Moerbeke, prolific translator of philosophical, medical and scientific texts. Moerbeke died in c.1286, and the colophon in the present manuscript describes the content as 'nove translationis'.

other_info: The illumination has been attributed to the Master of Dreux Budé. A key figure in 15th-century Parisian painting, the Master was named from a dismembered Passion Triptych executed for Dreux Budé, a lawyer who rose high in the service of Charles VII. His evident debt to Netherlandish painting and his close stylistic relationship with the Coëtivy Master encouraged Reynaud to identify him with André d’Ypres, master in Tournai in 1428 who moved from Amiens to Paris in or after 1443 (see F. Avril and N. Reynaud, Les manuscrits à peintures en France 1449-1520, 1993, p.56); the Coëtivy Master was identified with André’s son, Colin d’Amiens, who also settled in Paris. The subsequent discovery that André d’Ypres died in July 1450 in Mons after returning from a pilgrimage to Rome is consonant with the Master’s evident connection with van der Weyden, also in Rome that year, but has entailed a re-evaluation of an oeuvre usually considered to extend well into the 1450s (D. Vanwijnsberghe, ‘Du nouveau sur le peintre André d’Ypres, artiste du Nord installé à Paris’, Bulletin monumental, 158 (2000), pp.365-369; D. Thiébaut et al., Primitifs francais découvertes et redécouvertes, 2004, pp.92-101).

Its exceptional borders relate it to a small group of Hours of Amiens use, suggesting that the manuscript was mostly illuminated there; the French orthography indicates a Picard scribe. It was then probably sent to Paris for its miniatures - stylistically the first two relate to Rouen and the remainder to Paris, a combination more likely in Paris. There are numerous irregularly placed devices, some on blue shields, that might indicate ownership: the initials JG BL GY GM BJ GR; the St Andrew’s Cross and firesteels of the Dukes of Burgundy, as used by their Habsburg successors; the mottoes: JE ME PLAINS, AVE MARIA, GLORIA, AMOR; blue shields with sunbursts or silver ?stars between gold ?clouds, in varying numbers, and an illegible design in tarnished silver seem unlikely to be armorial bearings, although the sunburst and the illegible design reappear below the later miniatures on ff.88v and 89v. Below the two added miniatures with men praying, ff.86 and 87v, appears a shield gules, three keys or in fess, within an orle of chain or. One of these miniatures is St James, so the patron was perhaps named Jacques, which would fit with the JG and Y border initials. There are several 16th- and 17th-century inscriptions, some faint and some deliberately obscured, all relating to Normandy or families of Norman origin.

source_title: Catalogue de manuscrits avec miniatures des XIIIe au XVIIIe siècles
manuscript_binding: velours cramoisi,  tr. dor.
other_info: Il est orné de cinquante-neuf miniatures, de trente-six grandes lettres majuscules en couleur, avec ornements sur fond d'or, et de plus de milles lettres initiales moyennes et petites en or sur fond de couleur, disséminées dans le volume. Les pages contenant les miniatures et les grandes majuscules sont décorées d'un bel encadrement consistant en arabesques auxquels sont associés des perroquets, des paons et une grande variété d'oiseaux, des bustes d'hommes et de femmes émergeant de calices, de nombreux grotesques, d'anges chantant ou jouant de divers instruments, etc. En outre, les pages, au nombre de 300 environ, où figurent les initiales moyennes, ont un listel bordant la partie extérieure du texte duquel partent des branchages rehaussés de fleurettes en or et couvrant les marges sur trois côtés. Toutes ces peintures sont bien exécutées et d'une bonne conservation. Le volume s'ouvre par une miniature placée au v[erso] du premier f.  et représentant un écusson où sont peintes les armoiries de son premier possesseur: D'or, à la croix pattée de gueules cantonnée, au 1 et 4 d'une fleur de lis d'azur, au 2 et 3 d'une rose au naturel; écartelé d'argent plein. L'écu soutenu par deux lions d'or est surmonté d'un casque d'argent ayant pour cimier une aigle éployée de sable. Le tout est renfermé dans un cadre composé de fleurs sur fond or. Les autres miniatures se divisent en 37 grandes et 21 petites, ces dernières représentant des saints et des saintes. Les grandes, cintrées dans   le haut, et mesurant de 60 à 68 mill. de hauteur et environ 40 mill. de largeur, sont toutes placées aux versos des pages avec les rectos blancs. Nous en signalerons quelques-unes qui sortent un peu des sujets ordinairement représentés dans les livres d'Heures: Saint Louis, évêque de Toulouse, couvert d'un grand manteau bleu fleurdelisé. - Saint François d'Assises, agenouillé au pied de la croix, reçoit les stigmates qui partent des plaies de Notre-Seigneur et viennent s'incruster sur ses membres. - Moïse, entouré du peuple prosterné, reçoit des mains de Dieu les Tables de la loi. - La Mort, avec des ailes rouges, à cheval, décoche des flèches sur un groupe d'hommes et de femmes où tous les rangs de la société sont représentes; deux personnes gisent à terre. - Les Destinataires du volume, un homme et une femmes, sont agenouillés dans les champs et prient, les yeux tournés ver le Ciel où l'on voit le Père éternel, Jésus-Christ, la sainte Vierge et plusieurs saints entourés de rayons de gloire. - Un chœur d'anges dans une église. - Le Saint-Sacrement porté par un moine vêtu d'une robe blanche et d'un grand manteau bleu. - Les Destinataires cités co-dessus spot agenouillés dans une église; en face d'eux sont également agenouillés un homme et une femme plus âgés. - Sainte Hélène découvre la croix de Notre-Seigneur. L'impératrice, couronne en tête, vêtue d'un grand manteau bleu frangé d'or, regarde deux ouvriers qui creusent la terre; auprès d'elles se tiennent deux seigneurs. Quelques-uns de ces sujets et plusieurs de ceux des miniatures traditionnelles qui ornent ce manuscrit sont placés dans ce gracieux paysages avec des villes dans le lointain.

The French translation, commissioned by Charles V, was completed in 1375, and this copy of the first five books of the text was illuminated by the Orosius Master and his workshop in Paris, circa 1408-1410, possibly for Jean, duc de Berry. The first column miniature in the manuscript, marking the dedication to Charles V, depicts Raoul de Presles presenting his translation to the king (fol. 1r). A three-quarter-page miniature of the City of God and the City of the Pagans marks the beginning of the first book (fol. 5r) and double-column miniatures mark the beginning of each of the following books, as is true for many illuminated copies of this text. In addition, however, the first and second books of this manuscript are extensively illuminated with column miniatures at the beginning of each chapter, often drawing on the commentary for historical and literary source material. The text is written in two columns of textualis semi-quadrata script. At least one leaf is missing at the end of the volume, where the text breaks off near the end of the fifth book."

other_info: This is among the smallest examples known of the Paris “pocket” Bible. One tiny volume contains the entire biblical text, copied in a minute script on tissue-thin parchment and adorned with small painted initials, including five that are historiated. Its text belongs to the recension known as the Paris Bible, the direct ancestor of the sixteenth-century Clementine Vulgate. Although not in pristine condition, this is nonetheless an excellent example of a type of Bible of great importance both to the history of the Vulgate and to the history of the book in the Middle Ages.

other_info: fos. 238 + vi. With Parisian Calendar, added mid 13th cent. With additions of late 13th and early 14th centuries. The book was extensively repaired at the edges throughout in the early 14th century, and from the care and skill devoted to the repairs must have been a highly-valued possession. Decorative initials in red and blue pen-work and large initials in gold and colours of early 13th, late 13th and early 14th centuries. Miniature of the Crucifixion with seven saints, and one historiated initial of priest celebrating Mass, both with bar borders and ivy leaf decoration, added c. 1340, at the Canon of the Mass. A detailed account of the provenance and composition of the book is written by S.C. Cockerell on the first fly leaf. He acquired it in 1922 in two separate portions, A, of 186 leaves, and B, of 52 leaves. Exhibited at the Royal Academy, French Art, 1932, no. 751d., and in Paris, Palais National des Arts, 1937, Chefs-d'oeuvre de l'Art Francais, no. 746.

other_info:
The Lyghfield Bible
late 13th century
A pocket Bible probably produced in Northern France, probably Paris. 

With prologues of Jerome and Interpretation of Hebrew names, with 66 decorated initials, 72 historiated initials, 10 very large historiated initials and one full-page Genesis initial with seven scenes of the Life of Christ. 

With inscription identifying it as the Bible of Master Thomas Trussel, who is likely to be the man of that name who was appointed Archdeacon of Middlesex in 1331 but did not take up the office. 
Also faded inscription identifying it as the Bible of 'Dominus' William Lyghfield (Lighfyld'), a monk of Canterbury Christ Church. 
Lyghfield was one of the monks who received a pension at the Reformation, becoming a minor canon. 
A further faded inscription (legible only with UV light) almost certainly reads 'Christ Church Canterbury' in Latin. 

Purchased at auction at Bloomsbury Book Auctions in July 2018 from the Schoyen Collection with support from the National Heritage Memorial Fund, the Friends of Canterbury Cathedral, the Friends of the National Libraries and a private donation. 
Described in the auction catalogue as 'The Canterbury Trussel Bible' and identified one leaf as being missing.

(Size refers to text area only - see below):
"Illuminierte lateinische Pergamenthandschrift, Nord Frankreich, wahrscheinlich Paris, ca. 1440. 119 Blätter, 17 Zeilen pro Seite, braune Tinte, gotische Schrift, Schriftspiegel 95 x 64 mm, zahlreiche 2 - und 3-zeilige Initialen in Gold, Pink, Blau und Weiß; 17 drei Viertel Bordüren mit Blattranken in polychrome und Gold und fünf Miniaturen in Goldumrahmung..."
"Tls. berieb. u. schmutzfl. Loch b. der gr. Initiale unter der ersten Miniatur, tls. Randläsuren. - Die Miniaturen enthalten: die Verkündigung (f.13r), König David knieend neben seiner Harfe (f.21r), das Grab des Lazarus ( f.32v), die Kreuzigung (f.116r) und die Arma Christi (f.118v). - BOOK OF HOURS. Illuminated Latin manuscript on vellum. Northern French, likely Paris, c.1440. 119 leaves, 17 lines per page, brown ink, gothic bookhand, written space 95 x 64 mm, numerous 2- and 3-line initials in gold, pink, blue and white; 17 three-quarters borders of leafy tendrils in polychrome and gold; and FIVE ARCH-TOPPED MINIATURES in burnished gold frames. 19th century vellum. Some rubbing and soiling, hole to large initial under first miniature, occasional cropping to borders, binding defective. The miniatures comprise: the Annunciation (f.13r), King David kneeling beside his harp (f.21r), the tomb of Lazarus (f.32v), the Crucifixion (f.116r), and the Arma Christi (f.118v)." (from www.kiefer.de)

source_title: Medieval manuscripts from the collection of T.R. Buchanan in the Bodleian Library, Oxford [Bodleian Library, University of Oxford, 2001 (Peter Kidd)]
titles: Books of Hours, Use of Paris, in Latin and French
manuscript_binding: Sewn on three cords; green and brown end bands; bound in French 19th-c. dark brown or black leather over pasteboards, with contemporary pastedowns; spine with five false raised bands; gilt edges; boxed 1994
other_info:
[See cat. for additional notes, description, and bibliography.] Formerly Bodleian MS Lat. liturg. e. 23. ii+174+ii (endpapers front and back are modern parchment bifolia). 162-3 x 104-6 mm. (88-9 x 52-7 mm.). Quires of 8. Fine regular gothic book hand. Ruled in pale brown ink, with single vertical bounding lines extending the full height of the page. Calendar with 16 ruled lines per page [i.e. 15 written lines]. Script is smaller and markedly more angular from the start of the Office of the Dead (104r), but perhaps all by a single scribe. Shade of ink changes from quire to quire. Headings in red; marginal guides to the rubricator occasionally visible. Modern foliation, in pencil i-ii, 1-68a, 68b-175. | Contents include Calendar in French (type for Paris Books of Hours); Gosepl Pericope from John; Hours of the Virgin, Use of Paris, with three lessons at Matins; Hours of the Cross; Hours of the Holy Spirit; Penitential Psalms; Litany and collects ("Deus cui proprium est miserere semper et parcere" and "Fidelium deus omnium conditor et et redemptor"; Office of the Dead (Romanized Paris Use?); Prayers to the Virgin and to the Trinity in Latin and French ("O intemerata...orbis terrarum" (feminine forms), "Obsecro te..." (masculine forms), "Ave Maria gracia plena dominus tecum. Martir cum martiribus transgladiata...," "E tres certaine esperance...," "O sancta trinitas atque indiuisa vnitas uera...") [see cat. for descriptions and notes on contents]. | Decoration comprises 14 miniatures, most above four lines of text; figures with grisaille draperies, some in a rudimentary landscape with a ground line and trees, set against a diaper or patterned background; in a rectangular frame with gold bosses at the corners; above a three- or four-line initial, from which sprout ivy-leaf decoration surrounding the text and image on all four sides; sewing-holes on the outer margin of the first few miniatures, presumably from protective textile veils. 13r Pericope: St. John the Baptist holding Agnus Dei. 15r Hours of the Virgin, Matins: Annunciation. 27v Lauds: Visitation. 40r Prime: Nativity. 46v Terce: Annunciation to the Shepherds. 51r Sext: Adoration of the Magi. 55v None: Presentation in the Temple. 60v Vespers: Flight into Egypt. 68r Compline: Coronation of the Virgin. 73v Hours of the Cross: Crucifixion. 78r Hours of the Holy Spirit: Pentecost. 83v Penitential Psalms: God seated, turning away from the Tablets of the Old Law to bless covered chalice and wafer [cat. pl. 15]. 104r Office of the Dead: funeral service, with black-clad mourners, and clerics singing, on which an open book is inscribed in minute script with the Introit of the Mass of the Dead; 156r O intemerata: Virgin and Child enthroned, a laywoman in prayer before them [cat. pl. 16]. Pacht & Alexander relate the style to BnF MSS Fr. 22912-3, Augustine (Raoul de Presles) Cite de Dieu, 1376-80. | MS presumably made in Paris for the laywoman depicted on 156r (the prayer starting on this page uses feminine forms). Subsequently owned by an unidentified German prince-archbishop, whose armorial bookplate was transferred from previous binding to the present pastedown [cat. pl. 17]. Subsequent provenance includes an unidentified French owner and an unidentified French bookseller, before the acquisition by Messrs. T. & W. Boone.
MIGRATION_ISSUE: Last known location for this Entry is Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Buchanan e. 2, couldn't store this in the Manuscript record because there is none.
provenance: Thomas and William Boone (Firm); Buchanan, John; Buchanan, Thomas; Buchanan, T.R. (Thomas Ryburn), 1846-1911; Buchanan, E.O. (Emily Octavia), Mrs.; Bodleian Library, University of Oxford

source_title: Medieval manuscripts from the collection of T.R. Buchanan in the Bodleian Library, Oxford [Bodleian Library, University of Oxford, 2001 (Peter Kidd)]
titles: Books of Hours, Use of Paris, in Latin and French
manuscript_binding: Modern sewing probably on five cords, without endbands; recased in a 16th/17th-c. French limp parchment over parchment 'boards'; the covers tooled in gilt with foliate and interlace designs within framing lines; spine with 4(originally 6) sewing supports
other_info:
[See cat. for additional notes, description, and bibliography.] Formerly MS. Lat. liturg. e. 29. 134-6 x 94-7 mm (c. 77 x 47 mm). Modern pencil foliation i-ii, 1-154. 23 quires mostly of 8. Ruled in pale red ink (19 ruled lines, i.e. 18 written lines, except 17 ruled lines in quire XIX). The added leaves (1-3, 152) ruled with 19-21 lines in pale leadpoint. Lettre batarde in two different sizes of script, according to liturgical function. At least three main scribes, responsible for 16r-125v, 126r-133v (quire XIX, with different ruling), and the added leaves (1-3, 151-2) in a much later rounded humanist hand, perhaps imitating books printed in Roman type. Unclear whether the calendar may be by another scribe. | Contents. 1r-3v (quire I) Hymns added 16th/17th c. ("Veni sancte spiritus," "Veni creator spiritus," "Vexila regis prodeunt," "Veni redemtor gentium"). 4r-15v (quires II-III) Calendar, in French. 16r-21v Gospel Pericopes. 21v-25r "Oratio ad beatam mariam. Obsecro te..." 26r-71v Hours of the Virgin, Use of Paris. 72r "[Omnipotents sempiterne deus...]" starting imperfect at the fifth word due to the loss of a leaf after fol. 71. 73r-76v Hours of the Cross. 77r-80r Hours of the Holy Spirit (title on 76v). 80v ruled but blank. 81r-91v Seven Penitential Psalms. 91v-96r Litany and collects. 97r-136v Office of the Dead, Use of Paris, starting imperfect. 136v-137v Decotion, with heading in French "Pour les trespassez." 138r-150r Suffrages and other prayers. 151r-152v Hymns added 16th/17th c. ("Christe redemptor omnium ex patre patris...," "Christe qui lux es et dies..."). | Decoration. titles: Books of Hours, unidentified use, in Latin and French
artists: (Master of the Rohan Hours, workshop, style)
manuscript_binding: Sewn on three cords, with head- and (detached) tail-bands; bound in 17th(?)-c. parchment over thin pasteboards, stamped in gilt with an oval wreath in the center; spine in three compartments, each stamped in gilt; remains of two pairs of leather ties
other_info:
[See cat. for additional notes, description, and bibliography.] Formerly MS. Lat. liturg. e. 30. 171-3 x 136-8 mm (88 x 60 mm). Some miniatures cropped at top and close to border decoration. i (modern paper) + 189 + i (modern paper). Foliated in modern pencil i, 1-160a, 160b-189. 26 quires mostly of 8. Gothic bookhand in two sizes according to liturgical function, probably a single main scribe. The contemporary addition on 161v-162v (Suffrage to St. Barbara) is in a finer 15th-c. gothic bookhand, but in lesser-quality ink. | Contents. 1r-12v (quire I) Calendar, in French. 13r-17r Gospel Pericopes. 17r=25v Prayers to the Virgin ("Obsecro te," "O intemerata," "Salue mater dolorosa / Iuxta crucem lacrimosa"). 26r-75r Hours of the Virgin, unidentified use. 75v added texts relating to Sens (response and versicle and a suffrage to Saints Sabinianus and Potentianus of Sens). 76r-87v Penitential Psalms. 88r-94r (rubric on 87v) Litany and collects. 94v-101r (rubric on 94r) Hours of the Cross. 101v-107v (rubric on 101r) Hours of the Holy Spirit. 108r-113r Fifteen Joys of the Virgin, in French. 113v-116r (rubric on 113r The Seven Requests of Our Lord, in French. 116r-v Prayer to the Holy Cross, in French rhyming verse ("Saint uraie crois aouree / Qui du corps dieu fus a ornee"). 116v=118v Devotion to the Passion of Christ (John and Matthew). 118v-119v Verses of St. Bernard. 120r-161r Office of the Dead, use unidentified. 161v-162v added suffrage to St. Barbara. 163r-188r Suffrages, an unusually long series. | Decoration. 12 of an original at least 15 large fine miniatures, all but three above 4 lines of text; most with ogee-curved tops, though many cropped at top; one trefoil-shaped (94v) and one rounded (101v). Each with a three-sided frame usually of gold and painted foliage. Most damaged causing underdrawing to be visible in some plates. Miniatures in the style of the Master of the Rohan Hours (this MS is not mentioned in Meiss and Thomas). 13r Pericopes: St. John on Patmos. 26r Hours of the Virgin, Matins: Annunciation. 37v Lauds: Visitation. 53v Terce: Annunciation to shepherds. 63v Vespers: Flight into Egypt. 70r Compline: Coronation of the Virgin. 76r Penitential Psalms: David in Penitence. 94v Hours of the Cross: Crucifixion. 101v Hours of the Holy Spirit: Pentecost. 108r Fifteen Joys: Virgin nursing Child. 113v Seven Requests: The Last Judgement. 120r Office of the Dead: Funeral service. Vertical borders to every page, both sides of text, with sylized and semi-naturalistic plants. | Presumably made for the unidentified laywoman depicted on 108r. The unidentified use does not correspond with Troyes, Angers, or Paris, three uses for which the Rohan Master produced Books of Hours. Saints in the litany point towards the St.-Omer / St.-Bertin region. Subsequent provenance includes a near-contemporary owner, diocese of Sens. Symeon de Roussel, 1694, possibly responsible for present binding, inscribed on 188v [see cat.]. 19th-c. French owner inscribed "Les 7. alegresses de la Ste Vierge" 107v.

German(?) engraving of the Crucifixion, signed "G.N.," gilded and hand-colored. | Perhaps made for use in Paris, presumably still there when bound in the late 16th c.; fol. 1 perhaps added at the same time. 17th-c. red leather oval medallion inlaid on covers may replace an earlier owner's identification. source_title: Transformation of Knowledge, Early manuscripts from the collection of Lawrence J. Schoenberg
manuscript_binding: French humanistic script, brown ink, red rubrics, paragraph marks in gold, 2- to 4-line initials throughout in red and blue. 19th-century binding.
other_info: Tardif (c. 1440–c. 1500) was one of the foremost French humanists of the fifteenth century. His Basis grammaticae, of which this is the autograph, was written for his young pupil Charles Mariette, godson of Louis XI’s brother Charles de Guyenne. The text is a basic introduction to Latin grammar divided into eight parts, which consider nouns, pronouns, verbs, participles, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions and interjections. It also includes conjugation tables for four verbs, with some glosses in French for the verb amare (to love). The second half of the manuscript contains a commentary, in which Tardif explains his purpose – to give an account of Latin grammar “purged of the vices of the Barbarians”. This is the first French humanist grammar; it was printed in the early 1470s.

source_title: No. 90: Manuscripts and Printed Books from the Eighth to the Present Century
titles: Bible, in Latin. - Isaiah to Colossians, with the Prologues of St. Jerome
manuscript_binding: Binding of wooden boards in medieval style, broad back covered with pigskin and blind-tooled.
other_info:
Large folio (455 by 305 mm.), 177 leaves, signatures I-XVIII in tens (I [1-3] missing, text incomplete at end) 2 columns, headline (in red) and 40-41 lines to a page, written in a fine large Gothic hand. With 2 large miniatures of superlative quality representing St. Luke and the Decapitation of St. Paul, executed in burnished gold and colours, both within an initial P; 40 large ornamental initials in blue and red or in various colours; numerous smaller blue and red pen initials; beginnings and endings of the various books written in red. Ruling with plummet. 
A monument of French 13th century illuminating during the reign of St. Louis which produced one of the greatest works of medieval art, the Bible Moralisee, and, connected with it, a small group of other illuminated MSS., mainly executed for the Royal circle. It is to that celebrated Bible and one or two MSS. of the same group to which our MS. appears to be closely related. As Comte A. de Laborde has pointed out (La Bible Moralisee, V, pp. 170 et seq.), the group cannot be ascribed to a single hand or one atelier, but resemble each other in style and technique. The style of our MS. calls to mind especially the New Testament pictures in the Toledo MS. of the Bible Moralisee (op. cit. IV, plate 638 et seq.) and the Psalter of Queen Ingeborg at Chantilly (cf. J. Meurgey, Les Principaux MSS. du Musee Conde, pl. X-XIII) in which also the facial types have much in common with SS. Luke and Paul in our miniatures; the figure of the executioner in our Execution of St. Paul may also be compared to that of David on fol. 37v in the Psalter of Queen Ingeborg. Pierpont Morgan MS. 74, a Book of Hours, is another book with which our MS. shows unmistakable affinities. (cf. Burlington Fine Arts Club Catalogue, 1908, pl. 83).
provenance: Merton, Wilfred, 1888-1957; Martin Breslauer (firm)

source_title: No. 90: Manuscripts and Printed Books from the Eighth to the Present Century
titles: Book of Hours - Hours of the Virgin, Use of Paris
manuscript_binding: In an old velvet binding
other_info:
Illuminated MS. on vellum, executed in France, probably Paris, in the early part of the 15th century; 315 leaves (ff. 31 and 136 blank), 16mo. (92 by 65 mm., area of the written page c. 66 by 37 mm.), 13 lines, written in a good small Gothic hand, Calendar and some passages written in black and red. With 25 half-page miniatures (c. 47 by 33 mm.), surrounded by full-page borders with characteristic ivy-leaf decorations, and 1 miniature within an initial O. With 257 decorative initials with foliage ornamentations against a background of burnished gold, with ivy-leaf and flower borders, heightened with gold, extending to half, and often to the full length of the margins. Several thousand smaller gilt initials and line-endings, heightened with gold. 
A minuscule early 15th century Book of Hours of great charm and artistic interest; many of its miniatures show such unmistakeable affinities with the work of the celebrated Master of the Hours of the Marechal de Boucicaut and his atelier, that it must be assumed that they were painted by an artist who belonged to that workshop.

With 31 outstanding miniatures, 10 of these (c. 100 by 70 mm.) on full pages, surrounded by borders of flowers, foliage, animals and grotesques, and 22 smaller miniatures (between 50-60 by 45-50 mm.) all painted in colours both brilliant and delicately shaded, principally blue, azure, vermilion, orange, pink, mauve, green, golden-brown, yellow and white, with matt gold profusely applied; the borders richly heightened with burnished gold; decorated with c. 170 large blue initials heightened with white and filled with foliage in blue, orange and white, with backgrounds of burnished gold; many smaller gold initials against purple and light blue backgrounds, heightened with white, line-endings of purple and blue compartments heightened with burnished gold and white. 
In a magnificent French Renaissance binding of light brown calf, profusely gilt and heightened with silver; on sides a border of azured ovals enamelled with silver; large gilt centre-piece composed of strap work and arabesques painted silver, surrounded by a seme of diamond-shaped small tools, large azured and dotted arabesque corner-pieces heightened with silver; 5 raised bands on back, at head and tail a line of azured ovals, the other compartments filled with arabesques; gilt and gauffred edges.

Le volume est ornee de 18 superbe miniatures de la grandeur de la page comprises dans de riches bordures avec arabesques de feuillages, fleurs, fruits, oiseaux, etc. L'on y trouve feuillets 21 a 24, une oraison a la Vierge en vers francais. Il est orne d'un grand nombre de lettres initiales en or et en couleur; au recto de toutes les pages, se trouve une large bande egalement ornementee. Toutes les miniatures sont encadrees d'ornements en or et en couleurs representant des fleurs, des oiseaux, des insectes, des animaux et figures fantastiques, ainsi que des personnages en costume du XVe siecle. Dans l'ornementation de 6 de ces miniatures l'on voit au bas les armoiries de la famille Seguier. Tres beau manuscrit d'une grande fraicheur."
